Issued at 211 AM CDT Fri Sep 11 2026

A cold front is set to pass through the region this afternoon, 
turning winds to the northwest. Under the cold air advection regime, 
wind gusts may reach as high as 40 miles per hour, with perhaps a 
stray gust up to 45 miles per hour. Confidence on gusts reaching 45 
miles per hour (Wind Advisory criteria) is somewhat low at this 
point. HREF and REFS both do not give much credence to the 
possibility (<10% this afternoon) but NBM probabilities show a 
couple of hours of 10-20% chances to hit 45 miles per hour over 
north central South Dakota. Regardless of the exact probability, 
confidence is not high enough to issue a Wind Advisory today. The 
headline with a bit higher confidence is a Red Flag Warning, which 
is being issued with this forecast package for Jones, Lyman, and 
Buffalo counties. This are will see a period of humidity below 20 
percent this afternoon, which when combined with winds will create 
critical fire weather conditions. Further north humidity increases 
to 20-40%, which is still enough for elevated fire weather concerns 
and High to Very High Grassland Fire Danger this afternoon. 

The other point of concern with the cold front passing through will 
be convection over northeastern South Dakota and western Minnesota 
this afternoon. The latest model guidance trends towards storms 
firing over this area sometime between 20-22Z before quickly 
progressing eastward and out of the Aberdeen CWA as they intensify. 
This will leave a fairly short window in which severe weather could 
impact the area. Should storms fully develop within the Aberdeen 
forecast area, hail and wind will be the most likely severe threats. 
Hail in particular could prove to be significant, with a CAPE/Shear 
combo of roughly 3000+ J/kg and 30-40 knots in place. Also 
supporting the hail threat are mid-level lapse rates around 7.0-7.5 
C/km in the area. On the wind side of things, much of the area out 
ahead of the front will have upwards of 1000 J/kg of DCAPE in place 
and low-level lapse rates near dry-adiabatic to aid in gusts 
reaching the surface. Also can't quite rule out the potential for a 
tornado with these storms. Favorable ingredients include strong 
MLCAPE, helicity as high as 200 m2/s2, and low-level turning within 
the hodographs. The actual value of low-level shear leaves something 
to be desired (only about 20 to 25 knots, with perhaps some small 
pockets of a more ideal environment of 30 knots), but the main 
limiting factor to tornado potential will be LCLs over 1000m in most 
locations. However despite these limitations, it is not out of the 
question for these ingredients to line up in such a way that allows 
for tornadic development, but confidence is not high. It should be 
noted as well that a number of CAMs keep convection out of the 
Aberdeen CWA entirely. This is likely due to the limiting factor of 
a cap in place. The Potential Temperature difference between the 
surface and the warm layer is only about 5K at best, and there seems 
to be a bit of a spread in model confidence on the ability of that 
cap to be overcome or worn down through the day. All this to say 
that while this would definitely be a less likely outcome, it would 
not be entirely out of the question for the cap to hold and the 
Aberdeen area sees little to no convection today. The latest severe 
outlook from the Storm Prediction Center covers the areas east of 
the James River in a Slight to Marginal Risk. 

Temperatures behind the cold front will drop, with highs in the 60s 
across the forecast area expected over the weekend. These highs 5-10 
degrees below mid-September normals are expected to persist through 
at least the start of next week. The departing upper-level trough's 
right entrance region will move over the Northern Plains early 
Sunday, bringing a jet streak overhead. This will lead to some 
potential for rain showers Sunday morning across much of the 
forecast area. By Sunday afternoon, a brief ridge and surface high 
pressure center will build into the region, but both are expected to 
be fairly short-lived. 

Chances for rain return early next week as another upper-level 
trough moves over the Northern Plains. Divergence aloft from a jet 
streak will be the driving force for this system, as well as some 
help from an associated cold front. The below normal temperatures 
already in place out ahead of the front will help to form a fairly 
strong cap in place and likely significantly limiting deep 
convection through the profile. This in turn will all but eliminate 
chances for severe weather during this period, an assessment that 
mid-range severe probability models agree with. Still, non severe 
showers to perhaps a stray thunderstorm will be possible due to the 
divergence aloft (~50-60 knots of speed shear from roughly 700mb to 
300mb). Latest NBM probabilities of seeing half an inch of rain or
